AI video editor in Claude Code: 3 prompts, from an empty folder to a finished reel. SETUP (once) 1. Get the Claude app (claude.ai/download) and open the Code tab, not the browser. 2. Make a folder "AI Editor" with 3 folders inside: raw, references, done. 3. New chat in Code → Local → Select folder → AI Editor. Needs a paid Claude plan. PROMPT 1: TOOLS You're my video editor. We work in this folder: raw, references, done. Install and verify 5 tools: FFmpeg with libass (on Mac: ffmpeg-full, full path), faster-whisper for word-level subtitles, yt-dlp for references, Remotion, HyperFrames (npm package hyperframes). Check what's installed first. Official installs only (Homebrew, winget, npm/pip), Node.js 22+. Python packages go in a .venv here, Python 3.14 or older: pip install faster-whisper "av<19". Test each for real: burn a subtitle into a test clip, transcribe 5 seconds of audio. Show a table: tool, version, works or not. PROMPT 2: YOUR TASTE Here are reels whose editing I like: [link 1] [link 2] [link 3]. My format: [talking to camera / voiceover]. Download them with yt-dlp into references (for study only). Study each one frame by frame and by ear: pacing, shot length, pause cuts, subtitles, colors, graphics, transitions, music, the first 3 seconds. Take inspiration, but don't copy: no shots, text, logos or brand elements. Write my own style to style.md with exact values. Show it and ask what to change. PROMPT 3: EDIT My new recording is in raw. Edit it using style.md: 1. Transcribe with Whisper, word timestamps. Ask me about doubtful words before burning subtitles. 2. Cut pauses, slips and bad takes, keep the last good take. Check cut points by audio level. Keep pauses that serve the meaning, breaths and word endings. Don't speed up my voice. 3. Word-by-word subtitles in my style. 4. If references/music.mp3 exists, put it quietly under the voice. 5. Graphics only where they help. 6. Export 1080×1920 to done as draft-v1.mp4 plus edit-notes.md. Check the file yourself, then show me. I'll give edits in plain words; save each as draft-v2, draft-v3. No code words. Follow for my own editing style, coming next.

Heads up: - The spoken briefing uses a Cartesia or OpenAI API key (paid). Free: jarvis digest --text-only to read it (a local open source Kokoro voice is also in the code). - Gmail needs your own Google OAuth client (client_id:client_secret), the docs walk you through it. - Models run locally through Ollama, so your computer has to handle a local model. Cloud models are optional. - The installer asks about anonymous analytics - answer N if you don't want it. - The 40 emails in the video are an example, not a test result. AI can already cut, caption and format a clip for you. Free GitHub skills teach Claude the editing part in minutes. So why isn't everyone going viral off podcast clips? Because editing was never the hard part. Choosing the moment is. AI does not know which 47 seconds out of a two hour conversation deserve to become the clip. No context. No content intelligence. Here is how you build that layer. Scrape the latest 100 clips from the biggest podcast short form accounts. Steven Bartlett, Chris Williamson, Alex Hormozi, anyone running serious long form volume. Capture views, post date, duration, transcript, text overlay and format. Then scrape their original long form episodes and pull the complete transcripts with timestamps. The timestamps are non negotiable. They are what lets Claude match every clip back to the exact episode and the exact moment it came from. Now you reverse engineer the decision. Why those 47 seconds. Where the clip starts. What context got removed. Whether the payoff moved forward. What spoken hook, text overlay and format they used. And how it performed against that account's normal clips. Run enough of these and the patterns surface. Turn the patterns into a Claude skill that understands how the best podcast teams select and package their clips. Then hand it any new timestamped transcript. It returns the strongest moments, exact timestamps, hook options, text overlays, formats and editing instructions. The editing skill does the easy part. None of this needs new software. The tools exist. The clipping skills exist. The data is public. Nobody is assembling it into an intelligence layer. Impossible to fail does not mean every clip goes viral. It means every clip starts with real evidence, and every result makes the next selection smarter. Build the selection layer first. The edit is the easy bit.

Building an app with AI? Learn these 4 parts first Want to build an app with AI? Learn the four parts first: the front end, the back end, the database, and where AI fits in a modern app. When you ask ChatGPT or Claude to build you an app (vibe coding, no code), these four parts are what you're actually describing. Explained for complete beginners. We follow one customer message through an online coffee store app, start to finish: 1. Front end: everything the customer sees and taps. The screens, the buttons, the text box. It doesn't know prices or stock. It shows things and passes messages along. 2. Back end: runs on a server the customer never sees. This is where the business rules live: login, stock, prices, payments. The front end asks, the back end decides. 3. Database: where everything is saved, like a giant spreadsheet that never closes. Products, prices, customers, orders. Only the back end opens it, and it checks who's asking. 4. AI in the middle: the back end calls the AI model only for jobs that need understanding. Job one, turn a plain sentence ("a gift for my dad, he drinks it black, under $40") into a search. Job two, write the answer using only the real products the database sent back. The rule for building reliable AI apps: AI handles the words, the back end handles the facts and the money. Never let the AI make up prices or stock. Whole app in four lines: the front end shows, the back end decides, the database remembers, the AI understands and writes. If you want to go from understanding the four parts to building your own apps with AI, I teach it step by step, from complete beginner to real systems. I’ll share my entire local AI setup with Hermes and my Second Brain soon, but in short my Hermes agent bounces between Qwen 3.8 27b for easy stuff, and GPT OSS 120b for more complex tasks. But realistically you can do this with any model that’s capable of handling simple queries. I purchased an M5Stack Stopwatch which is essentially a tiny computer built on the ESP32-S3 chip. It already has Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and a motion sensor in it, all packed into a round AMOLED stopwatch. All it needs, is a firmware. When I was originally trying to get one of these, they were all coming directly from China, which would take weeks. Fortunately I found that DigiKey had stock of them and I was able to get my hands on it much quicker. From there, I gave Claude Code the following prompt to build the firmware and Hermes plugin: “Build a Hermes plugin and ESP32 firmware so I can chat with my Hermes agent from a little pet on my esp32’s screen over local Wi-Fi. Keep it simple and walk me through it.” But this only worked if you and your device were on the same local Wi-Fi network. So I built in a redundant direct Bluetooth connection using this prompt: “Add Bluetooth as a backup. If the pet can’t reach Hermes over Wi-Fi, have it switch to Bluetooth LE with my PC automatically, and switch back to Wi-Fi when it’s available again.” Then finally, I wanted to be able to access it from anywhere so I built in a Tailscale option that I can flip on whenever I’m away from my Hermes computer (like the personal AI server I’m building) using this prompt: “Add Tailscale so the pet can reach Hermes from any Wi-Fi, not just my home network. Put it behind an on/off switch in the pet’s settings and keep my local Wi-Fi setup working as before.” I strongly encourage you to try things out like this. Which AI app builder should you use? Lovable vs Bolt vs Replit vs Claude Code If you want to build an app with AI, here's which tool to use, and when to switch. There are two kinds: App builders, where you start. They run in your browser: you describe the app in a chat, it builds it, and it's running a minute later. Hosting and the database are built in. Lovable: the easiest; good-looking apps, fast. Free to try with 5 credits a day; every message uses credits. Bolt: same idea. Describe it, it builds it, it hosts it. Free to start with a monthly allowance. Replit: a full coding workspace under the chat. Free to try, but the free app goes offline after 30 days; the full builder is about $20 a month. Coding agents, for when you get serious. They work on the real code, on your own computer. Claude Code: comes with Claude Pro (about $20 a month). It's what I build with. Codex: OpenAI's version, with ChatGPT. On the $20 plan you get it in the app, your terminal and your code editor. Cursor sits in the middle: a code editor with AI built in. Heads-up: its cheaper plans now only run Grok models; for Claude or GPT you need the $30 plan. The move: start in Lovable, Bolt or Replit. Learn what an app is made of and prove your idea works. Then connect it to GitHub (Lovable and Bolt both let you), and keep building it in Claude Code or Codex. When it's time: when you spend more time fighting the tool than building your app. You don't need to code. But you do need to understand the front end, the back end and the database, how they connect, and how to keep your database secure. That's the upgrade. #vibecoding #aiagents #claude #lovable #replit #cursor #claudecode
